name: Question 10
problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
{y}^{″}+\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+1}{y}^{′}+(2+\operatorname{sin}⁡(x))y=0.
$$

Suppose ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are solutions and their Wronskian $W(x)$ satisfies $W(0)=10.$ What is $W(2)?$

$W(2)=$ {{field-1}}
worked_solution:
Abel's identity says that if ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are solutions of

$$
{y}^{″}+P(x){y}^{′}+Q(x)y=0,
$$

then their Wronskian $W(x)$ satisfies

$$
{W}^{′}(x)=-P(x)W(x).
$$

In our equation, the coefficient of ${y}^{′}$ is 

$$
P(x)=\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+1}.
$$

Substituting into Abel's identity gives

$$
{W}^{′}(x)=-\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+1}W(x).
$$

Now, we solve the first-order differential equation for $W:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{W}^{′} & =-\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+1}W \\ \frac{\text{d}W}{W} & =-\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+1}\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{\text{d}W}{W} & =\int -\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}x \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|W| & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)+K \\ |W| & ={e}^{K}({x}^{2}+1)^{-1} \\ W & =\frac{C}{{x}^{2}+1}\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a constant.

Next, we use the given value $W(0)=10$ to find $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}W(0) & =\frac{C}{{0}^{2}+1} \\ 10 & =C\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
W(x)=\frac{10}{{x}^{2}+1}.
$$

Finally, we compute $W(2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}W(2) & =\frac{10}{{2}^{2}+1}=2.\end{aligned}
$$
